body_en:
I heard a blogger break down the economy today — a genuinely clear-eyed take. Sharing it here.

1. The Myth of the K-Shaped Split

The biggest misconception about the economy today is an overfaith in the K-shaped story: the idea that as long as AI, semiconductors, and new energy — the rising arm of the K — shine bright enough, they can drag the whole economy out of the mud.

Hoping that a handful of cutting-edge tech companies going gangbusters can lift jobs and growth for the whole society is a fantasy detached from reality.

But the data punctures that fantasy: high-end industries simply cannot repeat the old path of the rich leading the rest to prosperity. The economy now faces a broad-based chill — one thin tech arm cannot hold up a sinking base.

2. New Quality Productive Forces Can't Carry the Jobs Base

Betting the entire recovery on new quality productive forces and hard tech is, in terms of both scale and logic, putting the cart before the horse.

Large models, high-end chips, commercial spaceflight — these frontier fields are intensive in capital and brainpower, not in labor. They can mint sky-high valuations in the primary market, dominate the conversation, and live comfortably off industry funds — but they can absorb almost none of the vast underlying workforce.

A small elite in high-barrier industries has captured the dividends of the era, while the traditional services, construction, and low-end manufacturing that actually underpin employment are shrinking faster in the cold.

Is the huge flexible workforce supposed to go find jobs in a large-model lab or a chip fab? Left out of the grand narrative, they have become the invisible cost of this illusion of localized prosperity.

3. A Rare Collapse in Fixed-Asset Investment

Even more glaring than jobs is the rare collapse in fixed-asset investment across society: down 4.1% year on year in the first five months of the year, with private and manufacturing investment hit especially hard. Expectations among micro-level actors have completely frozen.

Search more than 70 years of statistics, and fixed-asset investment has only ever gone negative twice: once in 1961, after the Great Leap Forward collapsed, and once in 1967, when factories shut down on a massive scale. The scale and ferocity of this round of decline have no precedent in modern economic history.

Fixed-asset investment is, at its core, whether companies are willing to build plants, buy equipment, and expand capacity. It is the clearest mirror of micro-level confidence. When that mirror falls off a cliff, it means private firms and foreign investors alike have voted with real money — for contraction and defense.

4. Not Growing Pains — a System-Wide Chill

This is not structural growing pains. It is a system-wide chill.

That systemic chill, plus the across-the-board withering of traditional industries, plus a true unemployment rate no one can even pin down — no handful of AI companies and new-energy firms can offset it with their local bright spots.

Conclusion

Seeing this baseline clearly is the precondition for any effective policy. Otherwise we stay trapped in the K-shaped illusion and miss the last window to save the economic base.
excerpt_en: The biggest misconception about the economy today is trusting the K-shaped story: that a few dazzling tech sectors can pull the whole economy out of the mud. The data says otherwise.
title_en: A Few Bright Spots Can't Offset a Systemic Chill
